lanes.label: Elsewhere in scripture
lanes.range: Topics in other books wired to this one

nodes.t: Hebrews: overview
nodes.d: The letter to the Hebrews presents Jesus as God's Son, greater than angels and Moses, our great high priest after Melchizedek who mediates a better covenant by one sacrifice, and calls readers to faith and endurance.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain in a few sentences what Hebrews teaches about Jesus and what the readers are told to do?
ev: Describe the main parts: the Son (1-2), Moses and rest (3-4), the high priest (4-7), the new covenant and sacrifice (8-10), faith (11), endurance and exhortations (12-13)

nodes.t: God has spoken by his Son
nodes.d: God who spoke by the prophets has in these last days spoken by his Son, heir of all things, maker of the worlds, radiance of his glory, who purged sins and sat at God's right hand, better than the angels.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what Hebrews 1:1-4 says about how God has spoken and who the Son is?
ev: List what 1:2-3 says about the Son
Say how 1:4-14 compares him with angels

nodes.t: Do not neglect so great salvation
nodes.d: Because the word spoken through angels was steadfast, the readers must give heed to the salvation first spoken by the Lord and confirmed by those who heard him, with God bearing witness by signs and wonders.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain the warning of 2:1-3 and why it is serious?
ev: State the question of 2:3
Say how the message was confirmed (2:3-4)

nodes.t: Jesus made like his brothers
nodes.d: Jesus, made a little lower than the angels, tasted death for everyone, shared flesh and blood to destroy the devil and free those enslaved by fear of death, and became a merciful and faithful high priest able to help the tempted.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why Jesus became like his brothers according to Hebrews 2:14-18?
ev: Say why he shared flesh and blood (2:14-15)
State what kind of high priest he is (2:17)

nodes.t: Christ greater than Moses
nodes.d: Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house, but Christ is faithful as a Son over his own house, and believers are that house if they hold fast.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain how the text says Christ is greater than Moses (3:3-6)?
ev: Compare servant and son in 3:5-6
Say what condition 3:6 states

nodes.t: Do not harden your hearts as in the wilderness
nodes.d: Quoting the warning that God swore the generation that provoked him in the wilderness would not enter his rest, the writer urges them to beware an evil heart of unbelief and to exhort one another daily.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what happened to those who came out of Egypt and what warning the writer draws (3:16-19)?
ev: Say why that generation could not enter (3:19)
Describe what 3:12-13 tells the readers to do

nodes.t: A rest remains for the people of God
nodes.d: The promise of entering God's rest still stands: the gospel preached to them did not profit those without faith, God rested on the seventh day, and a Sabbath rest remains for God's people, so they must labour to enter it.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the rest is that remains for God's people, and what warning goes with it (4:9-11)?
ev: Cite the creation rest mentioned in 4:4
State what remains for the people of God (4:9)
Say what the word of God does in 4:12

nodes.t: A great high priest who sympathises
nodes.d: We have a great high priest, Jesus the Son of God, who passed into the heavens and was tempted in all points like us yet without sin, so we may come boldly to the throne of grace.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why we may come boldly to the throne of grace (4:14-16)?
ev: Say how Jesus is like and unlike us (4:15)
State where we may come (4:16)

nodes.t: Called as high priest after Melchizedek's order
nodes.d: Every high priest is taken from men to offer gifts and sacrifices and is called of God as Aaron was; Christ was so called, learned obedience through suffering, and became the source of eternal salvation, a priest after the order of Melchizedek.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain how the text says Christ was called to be high priest (5:4-10)?
ev: List what a high priest does (5:1-3)
Say how Christ became a high priest (5:5-6, 5:10)

nodes.t: From milk to solid food: a warning and encouragement
nodes.d: The writer says the readers are dull of hearing and need milk, urges them to go on to maturity, warns about falling away after being enlightened, and is persuaded of better things, praising their work of love and urging diligence and patience.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the writer asks the readers to do in 6:1 and why (5:11-14)?
ev: Contrast milk and strong meat (5:12-14)
Describe the two earth pictures of 6:7-8
Say what the writer is persuaded of (6:9-10)

nodes.t: God's oath to Abraham: an anchor of the soul
nodes.d: God promised Abraham and confirmed it by an oath, swearing by himself; by two unchangeable things the heirs of promise have strong comfort, a hope like an anchor that enters within the veil where Jesus has gone as forerunner, a high priest after Melchizedek's order.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the text says about God's promise and oath to Abraham, and why it gives us hope (6:13-19)?
ev: State why God swore by himself (6:13)
Describe the anchor picture of 6:19-20

nodes.t: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest
nodes.d: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, met Abraham, blessed him and received tithes; this shows he is greater than Abraham and the Levites, and is made like the Son of God, abiding a priest continually.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what Hebrews 7:1-10 says about Melchizedek and why he is called greater than Abraham?
ev: Retell how 7:1-2 summarises Genesis 14
Explain the argument that the lesser is blessed by the greater (7:7)

nodes.t: Another priest, a change of law, an unchangeable priesthood
nodes.d: Because perfection did not come through the Levitical priesthood, another priest arose from Judah after the order of Melchizedek, by an oath and the power of an endless life; Jesus is surety of a better testament and lives to save to the uttermost and intercede.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why the writer says the priesthood had to change and what Jesus' priesthood is like (7:11-25)?
ev: State why another priest was needed (7:11)
Explain how Jesus differs from the many priests (7:23-27)

nodes.t: A better covenant: the new covenant promised
nodes.d: Jesus ministers in the true tabernacle as mediator of a better covenant on better promises; the writer cites the promise of a new covenant, in which God will write his laws on hearts, be their God, and remember their sins no more, making the first old.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe what the writer says God promised in the new covenant (8:8-12)?
ev: State what is better about the covenant (8:6)
List the promises of 8:10-12
Say what 8:13 says about the first covenant

nodes.t: The first covenant's tabernacle and ordinances
nodes.d: The first covenant had a worldly sanctuary with a first tent and Most Holy Place containing the ark, and only the high priest entered once a year with blood; the writer says the Holy Spirit signified this could not perfect the conscience until a time of reformation.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe the tabernacle arrangements and what they could not do (9:1-10)?
ev: Name items in the Holiest of all (9:3-4)
Say what the Holy Spirit showed by the arrangement (9:8)

nodes.t: Christ's own blood and the mediator of the new testament
nodes.d: Christ entered the heavenly sanctuary once by his own blood, obtained eternal redemption, and is the mediator of the new testament; the first was dedicated with blood, without shedding of blood there is no remission, and he will appear a second time without sin for salvation.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why the writer says Christ's blood does what the blood of bulls and goats could not (9:12-14)?
ev: Contrast animal blood and Christ's blood (9:12-14)
State what 9:22 says about blood and remission
Describe the two appearings in 9:26-28

nodes.t: One sacrifice for sins for ever
nodes.d: The law's repeated sacrifices could not take away sins, but Christ came to do God's will and by one offering of his body perfected for ever those who are sanctified; the writer again cites the covenant promise that sins will be remembered no more.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why Christ's single offering is enough according to Hebrews 10:10-18?
ev: Say why the old sacrifices were repeated (10:1-4)
State what Christ did and where he sat down (10:10-14)

nodes.t: Draw near with full assurance
nodes.d: Because of boldness to enter the holiest by the blood of Jesus, through the veil of his flesh, and with a great priest over God's house, believers are to draw near with a true heart, hold fast their hope, provoke one another to love and good works, and not stop meeting together.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the writer says believers should do because of Jesus' blood and high priesthood (10:19-25)?
ev: List the three "let us" calls in 10:22-24
Say what 10:25 warns against

nodes.t: Warning against wilful sin; endure and live by faith
nodes.d: The writer warns that no sacrifice remains for wilful sin after receiving the truth, reminds readers of their earlier endurance, and urges patience, since the just shall live by faith and they are not of those who draw back.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the writer asks the readers to remember and do in 10:32-39?
ev: Describe the warning of 10:26-29
State what the just shall do (10:38)
Tell what the readers endured before (10:32-34)

nodes.t: What faith is: Abel, Enoch and Noah
nodes.d: Faith is the substance of things hoped for and evidence of things unseen; by faith Abel offered a better sacrifice, Enoch was translated, and Noah built the ark; without faith it is impossible to please God.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what faith is (11:1) and give the example of Noah (11:7)?
ev: Recite or paraphrase 11:1
Say what 11:6 requires of one who comes to God
Name what each of Abel, Enoch and Noah did by faith

nodes.t: By faith Abraham, Sarah and the patriarchs
nodes.d: By faith Abraham went out not knowing where, sojourned as a stranger seeking a city built by God, Sara received strength to bear a child, Abraham offered Isaac, and Isaac, Jacob and Joseph acted in faith about things to come.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what Abraham did by faith and what the patriarchs were looking for (11:8-16)?
ev: Say what Abraham did by faith in 11:8-10 and 11:17-19
Name what Isaac, Jacob and Joseph did in 11:20-22
State what 11:13-16 says these people sought

nodes.t: By faith Moses, Israel and Rahab
nodes.d: By faith Moses' parents hid him, Moses chose affliction with God's people over Egypt's pleasures, kept the Passover, Israel crossed the Red Sea and the walls of Jericho fell, and Rahab was not destroyed.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe what Moses chose by faith and why (11:24-27)?
ev: List what Moses did by faith (11:24-28)
Name the two events of 11:29-30

nodes.t: The rest of the cloud: triumph and suffering by faith
nodes.d: The writer lists Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets, and describes those who conquered and those who suffered, none of whom received the promise without us.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the writer says about those who by faith suffered and had not yet received the promise (11:35-40)?
ev: Name some people in 11:32
Contrast the two kinds of experience in 11:33-38

nodes.t: Looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith
nodes.d: Surrounded by a cloud of witnesses, believers lay aside every weight and sin and run with patience, looking to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him and sat down at God's right hand.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what 12:1-2 tells believers to do and why they should look to Jesus?
ev: State what we lay aside and what we run (12:1)
Say what Jesus endured and where he is (12:2)

nodes.t: The Lord's discipline of his sons
nodes.d: The writer reminds readers that the Lord chastens those he loves as a father disciplines sons, for their profit and holiness, and that discipline afterwards yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why the writer says God's discipline is a sign of sonship (12:5-11)?
ev: State why God chastens (12:6, 12:10)
Describe the result in 12:11

nodes.t: Pursue peace and holiness; the example of Esau
nodes.d: The readers are to follow peace and holiness, watch against a root of bitterness, and not be like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal and later found no place of repentance though he sought the blessing with tears.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the writer says about Esau as a warning (12:15-17)?
ev: Say what we are to follow (12:14)
Tell what Esau did and what happened afterward (12:16-17)

nodes.t: Not Mount Sinai but Mount Zion
nodes.d: Believers have not come to the fearful mountain of Sinai but to mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to God, to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant and to the blood of sprinkling; they must not refuse the one who speaks, and receive a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain how Hebrews 12:18-24 contrasts Sinai with Zion and names Jesus there?
ev: Contrast the two mountains (12:18-24)
State what is said of the kingdom and of God (12:28-29)

nodes.t: Brotherly love, marriage and contentment
nodes.d: The writer calls for brotherly love and hospitality to strangers, remembering prisoners, honour in marriage, and a life free from covetousness because God has said he will never leave or forsake.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} name some practical commands in 13:1-5 and the promise that supports them?
ev: List the commands of 13:1-5
Say what promise supports contentment (13:5)

nodes.t: Leaders, Jesus outside the camp, and sacrifices of praise
nodes.d: Readers are to remember their leaders, avoid strange doctrines, go out to Jesus outside the camp bearing his reproach, seeking the city to come, and offer sacrifices of praise and doing good.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what it means to go to Jesus outside the camp and what sacrifices God is pleased with (13:12-16)?
ev: Recite 13:8
Say where Jesus suffered and what believers are to do (13:12-13)
List the sacrifices of 13:15-16

nodes.t: Obey leaders; blessing and farewell
nodes.d: The writer asks them to obey their leaders and pray for him, prays that the God of peace who raised Jesus through the blood of the everlasting covenant would equip them, and closes with news of Timothy and greetings.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe the prayer of 13:20-21 and what it says about Jesus?
ev: Say what the benediction asks of God (13:20-21)
Note the greeting from those of Italy (13:24)

nodes.t: Genesis: overview
nodes.d: Genesis runs from creation (1:1) to the death of Joseph in Egypt (50:26): creation, the fall, the flood, Babel, and the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} outline Genesis in order, from creation to Joseph in Egypt?
ev: Name the four main sections: creation, fall and flood, Abraham, and the patriarchs through Joseph
Say where the story begins (1:1) and ends (50:26)

nodes.t: God creates the world
nodes.d: God creates the heavens and the earth, and all that fills them, in six days, and rests on the seventh.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what God made on each day, and what happened on the seventh?
ev: Retell what God made on each of the six days
Say that God rested on the seventh day and blessed it

nodes.t: Cain and Abel
nodes.d: Cain murders his brother Abel after God accepts Abel's offering and not his own.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what Cain did and how God responded?
ev: Retell the story, including God's question to Cain (4:9)

nodes.t: Noah and the flood
nodes.d: God sees the wickedness of man, finds favour with Noah, and saves him and his household in the ark through the flood.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell the story of Noah and the ark?
ev: Retell why God sent the flood and how Noah and his family were saved
Say how Noah left the ark and what he did (8:20)

nodes.t: God calls Abram
nodes.d: God calls Abram to leave his country and promises to make him a great nation and bless all the families of the earth through him.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} list what God promised Abram in Genesis 12:1-3?
ev: State the promises of 12:1-3
Say that Abram went as the LORD told him

nodes.t: Isaac is born
nodes.d: God keeps his promise: Sarah bears Isaac to Abraham in his old age.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell how Isaac was born?
ev: Retell how God kept his promise

nodes.t: Abraham offers Isaac
nodes.d: God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac; God provides a ram in his place.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what God provided on the mountain?
ev: Retell the story, including 22:8 and 22:13-14

nodes.t: Jacob and Esau
nodes.d: Esau sells his birthright to Jacob, and Jacob later receives Isaac's blessing.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell how Jacob received the birthright and the blessing?
ev: Retell the birthright and blessing episodes
Note God's word to Rebekah in 25:23

nodes.t: God meant it for good: providence
nodes.d: Joseph tells his brothers that although they meant evil, God meant it for good (50:20); Paul teaches a similar confidence in Romans 8:28.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what Joseph meant in Genesis 50:20?
ev: Explain Genesis 50:20 in context
Compare it with Romans 8:28

nodes.t: From Adam to Noah: the first genealogy
nodes.d: Genesis 5 lists ten generations from Adam to Noah, repeating that each one lived a number of years and died, except Enoch, who walked with God and was not, for God took him. Lamech names his son Noah with a hope of comfort from the cursed ground.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} say what Genesis 5 tells us about Enoch, and why the chapter keeps repeating that each man died?
ev: Point out the repeated phrase 'and he died' in the chapter and the one exception in verse 24
Explain what Lamech hoped for when he named Noah (5:29)

nodes.t: Melchizedek blesses Abram
nodes.d: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, brings bread and wine and blesses Abram, who gives him tithes of all. Abram refuses the king of Sodom's goods, saying he has lifted his hand to the LORD, the most high God.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe what Melchizedek did for Abram and what Abram gave him?
ev: Say who Melchizedek is according to 14:18 and what he does and says
Explain why Abram refuses to take anything from the king of Sodom (14:22-23)

nodes.t: Hagar and Ishmael are sent away
nodes.d: After Isaac is weaned, Sarah sees Ishmael mocking and asks that he and Hagar be cast out. God tells Abraham that his seed will be called in Isaac but he will also make a nation of Ishmael; in the wilderness God hears the boy's voice and opens Hagar's eyes to a well.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what God promised about Ishmael, even as Isaac was the child of promise?
ev: Say what God told Abraham in 21:12-13
Describe how God provided for Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness (21:17-20)

nodes.t: Abraham buries Sarah at Machpelah
nodes.d: Sarah dies in Hebron, and Abraham, calling himself a stranger and sojourner, negotiates with the sons of Heth to buy the cave of Machpelah from Ephron for four hundred shekels of silver. He buries Sarah there.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain how Abraham came to own a piece of the promised land?
ev: Describe how Abraham obtained the burial place and what he paid (23:8-16)
Explain why a purchase of land in Canaan is notable in view of God's promise (cf. 13:15)

nodes.t: Israel's oath and the blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh
nodes.d: Israel makes Joseph swear to bury him with his fathers, then recalls God Almighty's promise at Luz and takes Ephraim and Manasseh as his own. He crosses his hands to bless the younger Ephraim first, over Joseph's objection, and says God will bring them back to the land of their fathers.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell how Jacob blessed Joseph's sons and what he said God would do for the family?
ev: Say where Jacob asked to be buried and who swore to do it (47:29-31)
Explain what was unusual about the way Jacob blessed the two boys (48:13-20)

nodes.t: Exodus: overview
nodes.d: Exodus tells of Israel enslaved in Egypt (1:1-14) and delivered through the plagues, Passover and the sea (chapters 7-15), then of the covenant at Sinai (19-24) and the tabernacle (25-40), ending with the glory of the LORD filling it (40:34-38).
nodes.q: Can {{name}} outline Exodus in order, from the bondage in Egypt to the glory filling the tabernacle?
ev: Name the main sections: bondage, deliverance, the journey to Sinai, the law and covenant, and the tabernacle
Say where Exodus begins (1:1) and ends (40:38)

nodes.t: Moses is born and drawn from the water
nodes.d: A Levite woman hides her baby son for three months, then places him in a basket of bulrushes by the river. Pharaoh's daughter finds him, has compassion, and the baby's own mother is paid to nurse him; he is named Moses.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} retell how baby Moses was saved from the river?
ev: Retell how the baby was hidden and found (2:2-6)
Say who nursed him and why that was surprising (2:7-9)
Explain the meaning of the name Moses given in 2:10

nodes.t: The Passover instituted
nodes.d: God tells Israel to take an unblemished lamb for each household on the tenth day, kill it at evening on the fourteenth, put its blood on the door posts and lintel, and eat it roasted in haste with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. When he sees the blood he will pass over; the day is to be kept as a memorial, and children are to be told what it means.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the Israelites did with the lamb and its blood, and what God promised?
ev: List what the lamb must be like and what was done with its blood (12:5-7)
Say what God promised when he saw the blood (12:13)
Say what parents were to tell their children (12:26-27)

nodes.t: Crossing the Red Sea
nodes.d: Pharaoh pursues Israel with chariots and traps them at the sea. Moses says to stand still and see the LORD's salvation; the LORD divides the sea, Israel walks through on dry ground, and the returning waters cover Pharaoh's army.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} retell the crossing of the sea and what Moses told the people to do?
ev: Say what the people said when they saw the Egyptians (14:10-12)
Say what Moses answered (14:13-14)
Say what happened to the Egyptians and how Israel responded (14:27-31)

nodes.t: The LORD descends on Mount Sinai
nodes.d: Israel is told to sanctify themselves and not to touch the mountain. On the third day there are thunders, lightning, a thick cloud and a loud trumpet, and the LORD descends on Sinai in fire; Moses goes up and is told to warn the people again.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe what happened when the LORD came down on Mount Sinai, and why bounds were set?
ev: Say how the people prepared (19:10-15)
Describe what happened on the third day (19:16-19)
Say what boundary was set and why (19:12, 19:21)

nodes.t: The covenant ratified with blood
nodes.d: Moses tells the people all the LORD's words and judgments, and they answer with one voice that they will do them. Moses writes the words, builds an altar and twelve pillars, reads the book of the covenant, and sprinkles the people with blood, saying it is the blood of the covenant the LORD has made with them.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what happened when the covenant was made in Exodus 24, and what Moses said as he sprinkled the blood?
ev: Say how the people answered (24:3, 24:7)
Say what Moses did with the blood and what he said (24:6-8)

nodes.t: The table and the golden lampstand
nodes.d: Instructions are given for a gold-covered table for the bread of the presence and a pure gold lampstand with seven lamps, made after the pattern shown on the mount.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} name the two furnishings made in 25:23-40?
ev: Say what was to be set on the table (25:30)
Say how many lamps the lampstand had (25:37)

nodes.t: The day of atonement
nodes.d: Leviticus 16 sets out how, after Nadab and Abihu died, Aaron enters the holy place once a year with offerings for himself and the people, blood on the mercy seat, and a live goat that carries the people's iniquities into the wilderness.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what happened on the day of atonement and what the two goats show?
ev: Explain why Aaron must not come into the holy place at just any time (16:2).
Describe the two goats and what happens to each.
State the date and the people's duty on that day (16:29-31).

nodes.t: Numbers: overview
nodes.d: Numbers follows Israel from Sinai through the wilderness: the census, camp and Levites, departure from Sinai, the rebellion at Kadesh and forty years of wandering, Balaam, a second census, and preparation on the plains of Moab for entering the land.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} give a short summary of where Israel starts and ends in Numbers?
ev: Describe the journey in Numbers in three stages: at Sinai, wandering, and on the plains of Moab.

nodes.t: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses
nodes.d: Numbers 12 tells how Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses, the LORD defends him as faithful in all his house and speaks to him mouth to mouth, Miriam becomes leprous, and Moses prays for her and she is shut out seven days.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the LORD said about Moses in Numbers 12:6-8?
ev: Say what Miriam and Aaron said and how the LORD described Moses.
Describe the outcome for Miriam and how Moses responded.

nodes.t: Israel refuses to enter the land
nodes.d: Numbers 14:1-25 records the people weeping and wishing to return to Egypt, Joshua and Caleb urging faith, the glory of the LORD appearing, Moses interceding with appeal to the LORD's mercy, and the LORD pardoning yet declaring that those who tested him will not see the land.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell how the people responded to the spies' report and how Moses prayed?
ev: Say what Joshua and Caleb told the people (14:7-9).
Describe Moses' prayer and the LORD's answer (14:13-23).

nodes.t: Deuteronomy: overview
nodes.d: Deuteronomy records Moses' words to Israel on the plains of Moab in the fortieth year: a review of the journey, the ten commandments and the call to love the LORD, the laws for life in the land, the covenant renewal with its blessings and curses, Moses' song and blessing, and his death.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain where Israel is and what Moses is doing throughout Deuteronomy?
ev: Describe Deuteronomy as Moses' speeches before Israel enters the land and name its main parts.

nodes.t: Hear the statutes: no images, remember Horeb
nodes.d: Deuteronomy 4:1-40 urges Israel to keep the statutes without adding or taking away, to remember the day at Horeb when they heard the voice from the fire and saw no form, to make no image, to beware of forgetting the covenant, and warns of exile yet promises that the LORD, merciful, will be found when sought.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why Moses told Israel to make no image of God?
ev: Say what Israel saw and did not see at Horeb and why that rules out images (4:12, 15-19).
Find the promise about seeking the LORD from exile (4:29-31).

nodes.t: Not for your righteousness: the calf recalled
nodes.d: Deuteronomy 9:1-10:11 has Moses tell Israel they will take the land not for their righteousness but for the nations' wickedness, recalling the golden calf, his breaking the tables and fasting forty days, his prayer for the people, and the second tables placed in the ark.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell how Moses used the golden calf to show Israel it did not earn the land?
ev: Say why Moses says Israel is not given the land for its righteousness (9:4-6).
Describe what Moses did after the calf and what the LORD wrote on the new tables (10:1-5).

nodes.t: Joshua commissioned; the law read every seven years
nodes.d: Deuteronomy 31 records Moses at 120 years old encouraging Israel and Joshua that the LORD goes before them and will not fail them, writing the law and giving it to the priests to read every seventh year, the LORD predicting Israel's turning away, and the book of the law placed beside the ark.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what Moses told Israel to do with the law after his death?
ev: Say what Moses told Joshua (31:7-8).
Say when and to whom the law is to be read (31:10-13).

nodes.t: The song of Moses
nodes.d: Deuteronomy 32:1-43 is a song that praises the LORD as the Rock whose work is perfect, recalls his care for Jacob in the wilderness, accuses Israel of forgetting him and worshipping other gods, tells of judgment, yet says vengeance is the LORD's and he will judge his people and be merciful to his land.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} summarize the song in three parts: the LORD's faithfulness, Israel's unfaithfulness and the LORD's judgment and mercy?
ev: Describe the picture of the LORD as the Rock in 32:3-4.
Summarize what Israel did in return for his care (32:15-18).

nodes.t: Joshua: overview
nodes.d: Joshua records Israel crossing the Jordan after Moses' death (1:1-2), taking and dividing the land, and Joshua's closing call to serve the LORD at Shechem, ending with his death (24:29).
nodes.q: Can {{name}} outline the book of Joshua from the crossing of the Jordan to the covenant at Shechem?
ev: Say how the book begins with the death of Moses and ends with the death of Joshua
Name the three parts: entering and conquering, dividing the land, and the farewell charges

nodes.t: The LORD commissions Joshua
nodes.d: After Moses dies, the LORD tells Joshua to lead the people over the Jordan, promises to be with him, and charges him to keep the law; Joshua then orders the people to prepare and the eastern tribes pledge their help.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what God said to Joshua at the start of the book?
ev: Retell what the LORD told Joshua after Moses died
Say what Joshua was told to do with the book of the law (1:7-8)
Explain what Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh promised (1:12-18)

nodes.t: Rahab hides the spies in Jericho
nodes.d: Joshua sends two men to Jericho, where Rahab hides them, confesses that the LORD is God in heaven and earth, and secures their oath to spare her family, marked by a scarlet cord.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what Rahab did for the spies and what they promised her?
ev: Retell how Rahab hid the spies
Say what Rahab had heard about the LORD (2:9-11)
Describe the promise the men made and the sign of the scarlet line (2:12-21)

nodes.t: The fall of Jericho
nodes.d: Israel marches round Jericho for seven days with the ark and trumpets, the wall falls at the shout, the city is devoted to destruction, and Rahab and her household are saved.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell how Jericho fell and who was saved?
ev: Retell the instructions for marching round Jericho (6:3-5)
Say what happened on the seventh day (6:15-20)
Explain why Rahab and her household were spared (6:22-25)

nodes.t: Judges: overview
nodes.d: Judges tells of Israel after Joshua's death, repeatedly falling into idolatry, being oppressed, crying out and being delivered by judges, and ends with the refrain that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe the cycle of sin, oppression, crying out and deliverance in Judges?
ev: Describe the repeating pattern in Judges 2:11-19
Name several judges and the enemies they faced
Say what 21:25 says about Israel at the end

nodes.t: Deborah, Barak and Jael
nodes.d: Under Jabin's oppression Deborah the prophetess calls Barak to fight Sisera; the LORD routs Sisera's chariots and Jael kills Sisera in her tent.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell how God gave victory over Sisera through Deborah, Barak and Jael?
ev: Retell why Deborah summoned Barak (4:6-7)
Say how the LORD gave victory (4:14-16)
Say what Jael did (4:17-22)

nodes.t: Gideon's three hundred
nodes.d: The LORD reduces Gideon's army to three hundred; after hearing a Midianite dream, Gideon surrounds the camp with trumpets, pitchers and lamps and the LORD sets the Midianites against each other.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell how Gideon defeated Midian with three hundred men?
ev: Say why the LORD reduced the army (7:2)
Describe how the three hundred attacked (7:16-22)

nodes.t: Jephthah is made head of Gilead
nodes.d: Jephthah, driven out by his half-brothers, is asked back by the elders of Gilead to fight Ammon; he first sends messengers recounting how Israel came to the land.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell how Jephthah became leader of Gilead?
ev: Say why Jephthah was expelled and why he was recalled (11:1-8)
Summarise his message to the king of Ammon (11:12-27)

nodes.t: The birth of Samson
nodes.d: The angel of the LORD tells Manoah's barren wife that she will bear a son who will be a Nazarite and begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines; Manoah offers a burnt offering and Samson is born.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what the angel of the LORD promised Manoah's wife?
ev: Say what the son was to avoid (13:4-5, 13:7)
Say what Manoah and his wife saw at the offering (13:19-21)

nodes.t: 2 Samuel: overview
nodes.d: 2 Samuel follows David from the news of Saul's death to his kingship over Judah and then all Israel, the LORD's promise of a lasting house, his sin with Bathsheba and its consequences in his own family, Absalom's and Sheba's revolts, and closing songs, warriors and a census.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} outline 2 Samuel from David's lament for Saul to the census at the end?
ev: Say how the book begins and what David did first
Name the promise in chapter 7
Name some consequences in David's family after chapter 11

nodes.t: The LORD's promise to David
nodes.d: David wishes to build a house for the ark; the LORD sends Nathan to say that he will make David a house, set up his offspring after him, establish his throne for ever, and be a father to his son; David then prays in thanks.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the LORD promised David through Nathan?
ev: Say what David wanted to do (7:2)
List what the LORD promised David (7:8-16)
Say how David responded (7:18-29)

nodes.t: Psalms: overview
nodes.d: The Psalms are 150 songs and prayers addressed to or about the LORD: cries for help, confession, thanksgiving, praise of his creation and rule, songs about the king, and meditation on his law; the book closes with calls to praise (146-150).
nodes.q: Can {{name}} name three kinds of psalm and read one verse from a psalm of each kind?
ev: Name several kinds of psalm (lament, thanksgiving, praise, royal, wisdom) and give one psalm number for each.

nodes.t: Psalm 2: the nations rage, the LORD’s king is set on Zion
nodes.d: The kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and his anointed, the LORD laughs and says he has set his king on Zion, declares him his Son, and warns the kings to serve the LORD with fear.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} outline Psalm 2 in its four parts and say what the kings are warned to do?
ev: List who rages against whom (2:1-3), who answers (2:4-6), and what the kings are told to do (2:10-12).

nodes.t: Psalm 8: what is man? the LORD’s majesty and man’s place
nodes.d: The speaker praises the LORD’s excellent name, considers the heavens, the moon and stars, and asks what man is that God remembers him, saying God made him a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory, with dominion over the works of his hands.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} read Psalm 8:3-6 and say what it teaches about God and man?
ev: Read 8:3-8 and list what is put under man’s dominion.

nodes.t: Psalm 22: my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
nodes.d: The speaker cries to God who seems far, is scorned and surrounded by enemies, his bones out of joint and garments divided, then declares God’s name in the congregation and says all the ends of the world shall remember and turn to the LORD.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe how Psalm 22 moves from the opening cry to the closing praise?
ev: Read 22:1-21 and list the pictures of suffering.
Read 22:22-31 and say how the psalm ends.

nodes.t: Psalm 40: I waited patiently for the LORD
nodes.d: The speaker waited patiently for the LORD who lifted him from a pit and put a new song in his mouth, says the LORD desires obedience and not sacrifice and offering, declares his righteousness to the congregation, and asks for help as poor and needy.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the speaker says in Psalm 40:6-8 about sacrifice and the LORD’s will?
ev: Read 40:1-3 and 40:6-8 and say what the LORD desires according to the speaker.

nodes.t: Psalm 45: a song for the king
nodes.d: The speaker addresses a king who is fairer than the sons of men, whose throne is for ever and whose sceptre is righteous; he is anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows, and a king’s daughter is brought to him.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe how the king and his throne are praised in Psalm 45?
ev: Read 45:1-7 and say what is said about the king and 45:10-15 about the bride.

nodes.t: Psalm 95: come, let us worship; harden not your heart
nodes.d: The psalm calls the people to sing to the LORD, the great King above all gods, who made the sea and dry land and is our shepherd; then it warns not to harden the heart as in the wilderness at Meribah, where God swore they should not enter his rest.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain the two parts of Psalm 95 and what the people are warned not to do?
ev: Read 95:1-7 and 95:8-11 and say what the call to worship and the warning each ask.

nodes.t: Psalms 96-99: the LORD reigns over all the earth
nodes.d: These psalms call the earth to sing a new song to the LORD, say all the gods of the nations are idols but the LORD made the heavens, repeat that the LORD reigns, and call the world to exalt him as holy and to rejoice at his coming to judge in righteousness.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what Psalms 96-99 say about the LORD’s reign and the gods of the nations?
ev: Find the phrase “the LORD reigneth” in 96:10, 97:1 and 99:1, and say what each psalm adds.

nodes.t: Psalm 102: the afflicted pours out his complaint; thou art the same
nodes.d: The afflicted speaker says his days are consumed like smoke and his bones cleave to his skin, he is like a pelican of the wilderness and a sparrow alone, but the LORD shall endure for ever, will build up Zion and hear the destitute, and the heavens will perish while he remains.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} contrast the speaker’s condition with the LORD’s endurance in Psalm 102?
ev: Read 102:1-11 and 102:12-22 and 102:23-28 and contrast the speaker with the LORD.

nodes.t: Psalm 104: the LORD’s creation and provision
nodes.d: The speaker blesses the LORD for stretching out the heavens, setting the earth’s foundations, sending springs and grass for the cattle, giving the beasts and birds their places, and says all creatures look to him for food and live when he sends his spirit.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what Psalm 104 says about God’s care for creation and every creature?
ev: Read 104:1-9, 104:10-23 and 104:24-30 and list what the LORD provides.

nodes.t: Psalm 110: sit at my right hand; a priest after Melchizedek
nodes.d: The LORD says to the speaker’s Lord to sit at his right hand until his enemies are his footstool; he is a king sent to rule from Zion and a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek, sworn by the LORD.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} read Psalm 110:1 and 110:4 and say what the LORD says to the speaker’s Lord?
ev: Read 110:1-4 and say who speaks and to whom, and what is sworn.

nodes.t: Psalms 117-118: his mercy endureth for ever; the stone the builders refused
nodes.d: Psalm 117 calls all nations to praise the LORD for his great mercy and truth; Psalm 118 calls Israel to say his mercy endures for ever, tells of being delivered from distress, says it is better to trust the LORD than man, speaks of the stone the builders refused, and ends with giving thanks.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain the refrain “his mercy endureth for ever” and the picture in Psalm 118:22-23?
ev: Read 118:5-9, 118:19-24 and 118:26-29 and list what is said about the LORD and the gate.

nodes.t: Proverbs: overview
nodes.d: Proverbs begins with the proverbs of Solomon son of David (1:1), sets out a father’s teaching about wisdom and folly (1-9), gathers many short sayings (10-29), and ends with the words of Agur (30) and of king Lemuel (31).
nodes.q: Can {{name}} name the main sections of Proverbs and who is named as the source of each?
ev: Describe the main sections of Proverbs: 1-9, 10-22, 22-24, 25-29, 30, 31.

nodes.t: Trust in the LORD with all your heart
nodes.d: The father tells his son to keep his commandments, trust in the LORD and not lean on his own understanding, accept the LORD’s correction, value wisdom above silver and gold, and do good to his neighbour.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain Proverbs 3:5-6 and give one example of leaning on one’s own understanding?
ev: Read 3:5-6 and say what the son is told to do and what the LORD does.
Find 3:11-12 and say what it says about correction.

nodes.t: Maher-shalal-hash-baz and the Assyrian flood
nodes.d: Isaiah writes a name-sign for a son, the LORD warns that the king of Assyria will flood Judah, tells Isaiah not to fear what the people fear, and calls him to the law and testimony instead of mediums.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why the LORD says to sanctify him rather than fear what the people fear in Isaiah 8:11-13?
ev: Explain the meaning of the child's name sign in 8:1-4
Say whom Isaiah is told to fear and sanctify (8:12-13)
Explain the contrast between the law and testimony and consulting the dead (8:19-20)

nodes.t: Jeremiah: overview
nodes.d: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, a priest of Anathoth, receives the word of the LORD from the thirteenth year of Josiah to the exile after Zedekiah's eleventh year, warning Judah of judgment from the north and promising restoration and a new covenant.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} say who Jeremiah was and during whose reigns the word of the LORD came to him according to Jeremiah 1:1-3?
ev: Name the kings during whose reigns the word came (Jeremiah 1:1-3)
Explain that the book is not arranged only in the order of the events it describes, using examples from its dates

nodes.t: The new covenant
nodes.d: The LORD promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah, unlike the one broken after the exodus: he will write his law on their hearts, they will all know him, and he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what is new about the covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31-34?
ev: Say whom the covenant is made with and what it is unlike (31:31-32)
Describe what the LORD does in 31:33
Quote the promise of forgiveness in 31:34

nodes.t: Habakkuk: overview
nodes.d: The burden Habakkuk saw: his complaints about violence in Judah and the LORD's answers, the vision to wait for in which the just live by faith, woes on the proud, and a prayer ending in rejoicing in the LORD.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain how Habakkuk moves from complaint to rejoicing?
ev: Describe the pattern of complaint and answer in chapters 1-2
Say how the book ends (3:17-19)

nodes.t: The vision to wait for; the just live by faith
nodes.d: Habakkuk stands on his watch; the LORD tells him to write the vision, which will surely come though it tarries, and contrasts the proud, whose soul is not upright, with the just, who shall live by his faith.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain the contrast of Habakkuk 2:4 and say what the LORD tells Habakkuk to do with the vision?
ev: Say what Habakkuk does and what the LORD tells him to do (2:1-3)
Read 2:4 and state the contrast
Find where Paul cites it (Romans 1:17)
